questions.question: A loan company says its AI decisions have "human oversight" because one staff member approves about 500 AI decisions every hour and cannot change any of them. What is the main problem?
options: There is no problem, because a person approves every decision.
The reviewer does not have enough time or authority, so the oversight is not real.
The problem is only the speed of the AI, not the review.
Human oversight is only needed for chatbots, not for loan decisions.
questions.explanation: Real oversight needs a person with enough time, knowledge and authority to question and change the decision. The most tempting wrong option is that there is no problem because a person approves every decision. A reviewer with no time and no power only confirms what the machine already decided.

questions.question: Which item is the best example of turning a responsible-AI principle into a practical checklist question?
options: "AI should respect human values."
"Read the full text of an international framework once a year."
"Our company supports responsible AI."
"Have I removed all personal and client-confidential details from my prompt?"
questions.explanation: A checklist question is specific and can be answered yes or no for a real task, as this privacy question can. The most tempting wrong option is "AI should respect human values". It sounds like a principle, but it is too general to check on a single task.

questions.question: You want to test whether a chatbot writes job references differently for different genders. Which test design is best?
options: Use two prompts with identical CVs that change only the name, run each in a new chat several times, and record every answer.
Use two prompts with different names, different ages and different CVs, and run each once.
Ask the chatbot directly whether it is biased against women.
Run one pair of prompts once and report any difference as proof of bias.
questions.explanation: A paired prompt changes only one detail, and repeating it in new chats shows whether a difference is a pattern or random. The most tempting wrong option is running one pair once. Chatbot answers vary each time, so one difference is a limited result, not proof of bias.

questions.question: A chatbot often gives slightly wrong opening hours (high likelihood, low impact). Rarely, it tells users with chest pain to "rest and wait" (low likelihood, high impact). Which should usually get attention first?
options: The opening hours, because they happen more often.
Neither, because both risks are already known.
The chest-pain advice, because its impact is serious even though it is rare.
Both equally, because all risks have the same priority.
questions.explanation: A risk matrix weighs both likelihood and impact, and a rare but serious safety risk usually deserves early action. The most tempting wrong option is the opening hours because they happen more often. Frequency alone does not decide priority when the other risk could seriously harm someone.

questions.question: Which recommendation is written best for an audit report?
options: "Make the tool fairer and safer."
"The customer-service team lead checks every AI-drafted refund reply before it is sent, starting next month."
"Replace the tool with a perfect system that never makes mistakes."
"Someone should look at the problems we found at some point."
questions.explanation: A good recommendation is specific, realistic and assigned to someone, with a time where possible. The most tempting wrong option is "Make the tool fairer and safer", because it points in the right direction. But it does not say what should happen, who does it or when, so nobody can act on it.
